name: Kyiv
info: Kyiv, also spelt Kiev, is the capital of Ukraine, on both banks of the Dnieper. Traditionally dated to 482 CE, it was the capital of Kievan Rus', then a provincial city under several powers, and a Soviet and Ukrainian capital.

facts.founded: The date is debated: 482 CE is the traditional date, archaeological data indicates the 6th or 7th century, and some researchers date the founding as late as the late 9th century. According to the Primary Chronicle the brothers Kyi, Shchek and Khoryv and their sister Lybid founded it.
facts.where: On both banks of the Dnieper River in north-central Ukraine, on the hills of the western bank, close to the mouth of the Desna.
facts.known: Capital of Kievan Rus'; the baptism of 988; St Sophia Cathedral and the Monastery of the Caves; the Mongol destruction of 1240; the Kyiv-Mohyla Academy; capital of Soviet and then independent Ukraine; Babi Yar
facts.today: Kyiv is the capital and most populous city of Ukraine, a city with the legal status of a region.

t: Kyiv was the capital of Kievan Rus' from the late 9th century, reached its height in the middle of the 11th century under Yaroslav the Wise, and was left in ruins by the Mongols on 6 December 1240.
For centuries afterwards it was a provincial city under the Golden Horde, Lithuania, Poland and Russia, yet it remained the seat of the Orthodox metropolitan and a centre of Ukrainian culture.

It became the capital of short-lived Ukrainian states in 1917, of Soviet Ukraine in 1934 and of independent Ukraine in 1991, and it suffered greatly in the famine of 1932 and 1933 and in the Second World War.
dyk: Between 1146 and 1246 Kyiv changed hands 47 times and was ruled by 24 princes, 35 of whose tenures lasted less than a year.
ev: The traditional date of the city's founding, celebrated as its 1,500th anniversary in 1982
Prince Volodymyr I accepts Christianity and orders the people of Kyiv to be baptised in the Dnieper
An army of eleven princes sent by Andrei Bogolyubsky sacks the city for three days
Batu Khan's Mongols besiege Kyiv and destroy it
After the Battle of Blue Waters Kyiv passes to the Grand Duchy of Lithuania
The Truce of Andrusovo cedes Kyiv to the Tsardom of Russia
Nazi Germany occupies the city, and nearly 34,000 Jews are killed at Babi Yar
Ukraine declares independence in Kyiv, which becomes the capital of an independent state

sections.origins:
Kyiv stands on the Dnieper, on the hills of its western bank. The first known humans in the region lived there in the late Palaeolithic, and the people of the Bronze Age belonged to the Trypillian culture, whose artefacts have been found in the area. In the early Iron Age tribes who farmed, kept livestock and traded with the Scythians and the states of the northern Black Sea coast settled around Kyiv. Finds of Roman coins of the 2nd to 4th centuries suggest trade with the eastern provinces of the Roman Empire.

Scholars continue to debate when the city was founded. The traditional date is 482 CE, so the city celebrated its 1,500th anniversary in 1982. Archaeological data indicates the 6th or 7th century, and some researchers date the founding as late as the late 9th century. Tree-ring analysis of log dwellings in Podil has found evidence of settlement only as far back as 887, and Omeljan Pritsak writes that Kyiv did not exist as a town before the last quarter of the 9th century.

The Primary Chronicle tells that the Polyanian brothers Kyi, Shchek and Khoryv and their sister Lybid founded the town on three hills and named it after Kyi. Another legend holds that Saint Andrew passed through the area in the 1st century and erected a cross where a church was later built. The earliest more reliable evidence suggests an early medieval Slavic settlement that paid tribute to the Khazars, on the route between Scandinavia and Constantinople.
sections.growth:
As the capital of Kievan Rus' the city stood on the trade route between the Varangians and the Greeks. In 968 it withstood a siege by the nomadic Pechenegs. By 1000 CE it had a population of 45,000, and Thietmar of Merseburg, describing it in his chronicle from 1017, recorded over 400 churches and 8 markets. Yaroslav the Wise, Grand Prince from 1019 to 1054, built St Sophia Cathedral, and the middle of the 11th century was the city's political and cultural height. An Armenian merchant factory was based there from the 11th century until the Mongol invasions.

Kyiv had a reputation as one of the largest cities in the world. Before the Mongol invasion its population was about 35,000 to 40,000 according to Orest Subtelny, and 36,000 to 50,000 at the end of the 12th century according to Janet L. B. Martin.

After 1240 Kyiv was for centuries a provincial capital of marginal importance, though it remained the seat of the Orthodox metropolitan. In the early 17th century the Monastery of the Caves became a centre of Orthodox cultural revival, and in 1632 Peter Mogila founded the Kyiv-Mohyla Academy. In the late 19th century, during the Russian industrial revolution, Kyiv became a trade and transport centre that exported sugar and grain by railway and on the Dnieper. By 1900 it had a population of 250,000, and in 1892 the first electric tram line of the Russian Empire had opened there.
sections.rulers:
According to the Primary Chronicle, Oleg the Wise conquered Kyiv in 881 or 882. Omeljan Pritsak and Constantine Zuckerman dispute this and hold that Khazar rule continued as late as the 920s, and other historians suggest that Magyar tribes ruled the city between 840 and 878. From Oleg's seizure Kyiv was the capital of Kievan Rus', ruled by the Varangian Rurikid dynasty, which gradually became Slavicised. The inner Principality of Kyiv emerged in 1132. After 1240 the Golden Horde ruled the city through yarlyks issued by Mongol rulers. In 1362 Algirdas defeated a Golden Horde army at Blue Waters and took Kyiv into the Grand Duchy of Lithuania. In 1471 the principality was abolished and a voivodeship set up, and in 1569, under the Union of Lublin, the city passed to the Crown of the Kingdom of Poland.

Bohdan Khmelnytsky's Cossacks entered the city during their uprising. By the Truce of Andrusovo of 31 January 1667 the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth ceded Kyiv to Russia, on paper for two years, and the Eternal Peace of 1686 acknowledged the existing situation. None of the Polish-Russian treaties concerning the city has been ratified. Catherine the Great abolished Ukraine's autonomy in 1775.

In 1917 the Central Rada was established in Kyiv, and on 7 November 1917 it proclaimed the Ukrainian People's Republic with its capital there. The city changed hands sixteen times from the end of 1918 to August 1920. It was part of the Ukrainian Soviet Socialist Republic, its capital from 1934, until 1991.
sections.life:
From the late 9th century Kyiv mixed pagan Slavic, Norse, Christian, Islamic and Jewish traditions. In 988 Prince Volodymyr I ordered the residents to accept baptism in the Dnieper, and Christianity became dominant, with Church Slavonic as the literary standard. Under Lithuanian rule the core of the city lay in Podil, and a castle with 18 towers stood on Zamkova Hora. From 1494 the city's autonomy under Magdeburg rights grew, and a charter of 1516 finished the process. Tsar Nicholas I abolished the Magdeburg law on 23 December 1834, the year St Vladimir University was founded.

Jews are first mentioned in Kyiv in a 10th-century letter. Sigismund II Augustus granted them equal rights in the 16th century. They were expelled in 1654 and probably could not settle again until the early 1790s, and in 1836 the Pale of Settlement banned them from the city, though a large Jewish community emerged in the 19th century. On the eve of the First World War there were over 81,000 Jews in Kyiv. Poles were an important element in the 19th century. The Russian census of 1897 recorded about 240,000 people, of whom about 56% spoke Russian, 23% Ukrainian and 7% Polish. Tsar Alexis expelled the local Armenians in 1660.

The names of the city's districts follow its relief: Podil means lower, Pechersk means caves. The Left Bank on the east side of the Dnieper was built up only in the 20th century.
sections.crises:
In 1169 an army of eleven princes sent by Andrei Bogolyubsky sacked Kyiv for three days and left the old town and the prince's hall in ruins. In 1203 Rurik Rostislavich and his Kipchak allies captured and burned it, and in the 1230s Rus' princes besieged and ravaged it several times. On 6 December 1240 Batu Khan's Mongols besieged the city and destroyed it. According to one account the garrison had thrown down the bodies of the Mongol envoys, and in revenge the Mongols broke down the gates, slaughtered much of the population and razed the city. In 1482 Crimean Tatars sacked and burned much of it, and in 1811 the Great Fire of Podil devastated it.

In the 1930s Kyiv suffered the Holodomor of 1932 and 1933 and the purges, with mass executions at Babi Yar and in the Bykivnia forest. In the Battle of Kyiv in 1941 the Axis killed or captured more than 600,000 Soviet soldiers. German occupation lasted from 19 September 1941 to 6 November 1943. Soon after it began, mines or explosives set by the Soviet side destroyed most of the buildings on the Khreshchatyk, which burned for days. On 29 and 30 September 1941 nearly 34,000 Jews of Kyiv were massacred at Babi Yar, and it is estimated that the Germans killed more than 100,000 people there during the war. A pogrom in September 1945 left five Jews dead. The Chernobyl accident of 1986 occurred about 100 km north of the city.

In February 2022 Russian forces attempted to seize Kyiv and were repelled on its outskirts. The Russian offensive in Kyiv Oblast was defeated on 2 April 2022, and air strikes on the city have continued since.
sections.legacy:
The Cathedral of St Sophia and the Kyiv Pechersk Lavra are recognised by UNESCO as a World Heritage Site, and in September 2023 the World Heritage Committee placed them on the List of World Heritage in Danger because of the war. Other landmarks include the Golden Gate, the Mariinskyi Palace, built from 1745 to 1752, and the Brodsky Choral Synagogue. Kyiv was a cradle of the Christianisation of Rus' and remained a centre of Eastern Orthodoxy, a pilgrimage destination for centuries. The Kyiv-Mohyla Academy is the oldest of the city's universities, and Shevchenko University, founded in 1834, is the oldest in continuous operation.

Kyiv has been a centre of invention and of Ukrainian public life. Igor Sikorsky, born there, built and tested the world's first helicopter in the city. The Ukrainian parliament proclaimed the Declaration of Independence in Kyiv on 24 August 1991. Mass demonstrations in support of the Orange Revolution followed in 2004 and 2005, and from November 2013 to February 2014 central Kyiv was the main location of Euromaidan, also called the Revolution of Dignity.

Kyiv is the official romanised Ukrainian spelling, while Kiev is the traditional English name. The city had 2,611,327 people at the census of 2001, of whom 82.2% were Ukrainians, and has nearly three million today.

summary: Kyiv, on the Dnieper, was the capital of Kievan Rus' and was destroyed by the Mongols in 1240. It later served as a provincial city under several powers, then as the capital of Soviet Ukraine from 1934 and of independent Ukraine from 1991.
references: Natalia Oleksijivna Bilous, Київ наприкінці XIV — у першій половині XVII століття. Міська влада і самоврядування (Publishing House Kyiv-Mohyla Academy, 2008)
Paul Robert Magocsi, A History of Ukraine: The Land and Its Peoples (University of Toronto Press, 1996)
notes: FOUNDING: the articles disagree or hedge. 482 CE is traditional (1,500th anniversary 1982); archaeology 6th or 7th century (Kyiv article); dendrochronology only to 887 and Pritsak: no town before the last quarter of the 9th century (History article). I used start 482, circa true, and gave all versions in origins.

CONQUEST BY OLEG: History article 881/2, Kyiv article 882 (murder of Askold and Dir). Written as 881 or 882. Magyar rule 840-878 and the 840 fortress claim (Kyiv article) given only as 'other historians suggest'; the 840 date and the Hungarian brothers left out.
COSSACKS ENTERING KYIV: History article 1648, Kyiv article 1649. Year left out.

POGROMS: History article says 1881 and 1905 with about 100 Jewish dead; Kyiv article says 1882 and 1905. Left out of the text entirely, as were the death figure and the year. 1874 census: 127,251 (History) against 127,205 (Kyiv): not used.

BABI YAR: History article says at least 33,771 Jews killed on two days in September 1941 by SS Einsatzgruppen according to their own reports, plus perhaps as many as 60,000 more; Kyiv article says nearly 34,000 on 29 and 30 September and more than 100,000 of all groups during the war. I used 'nearly 34,000' and the 'more than 100,000' estimate, attributed. The Kyiv article says 'allegedly in response to the NKVD'; left out.

KHRESHCHATYK: History article says the Red Army planted over ten thousand mines and detonated them on 24 September; Kyiv article says NKVD officers dynamited most buildings after the occupation began; 25,000 left homeless. Written neutrally as 'mines or explosives set by the Soviet side'.
MONGOL STORY: the garrison throwing down the envoys' bodies is only in the History article; given as 'according to one account'. Death toll not given in either article.

MOHYLA: History article says Peter Mogila 'established' the academy in 1632; Kyiv article says it was a brotherhood school later known as the Mohyla Collegium and that the Academy was founded in 1632 as a theological school. Written as Mogila founding it in 1632 as in the History article.
ELECTRIC TRAM: 1892 in both articles; the Kyiv article calls it the third in the world, left out. Sikorsky 'built and tested the world's first helicopter in Kyiv' is the History article's claim.
LANGUAGES 1897: History 56/23/12.5/7/1; Kyiv article 56/23/13/7/1 for the same census. Yiddish share left out.

RECENT WAR (as instructed): 2014 and 2022 told as bare dated facts. Air-strike lists, casualty figures and the Kyiv article's 'as of' statements left out. The History article lists a strike dated 'July 2 2026' and counts '30 strikes as of October 2023'; not used. UNESCO's Sept 2023 listing given as a bare fact with its stated reason.
POPULATION TODAY: the Kyiv article gives 2,952,301 'as of January 2022'; written as 'nearly three million today' without the year. The 2001 census figures are as given.

LEFT OUT: tourism, sport, economy, transport, twin towns, climate, notable people, the Ptolemy 'Azagarium' and Sambat discussions, the Askold and Dir passage beyond Oleg, the Pritsak/Zuckerman letters beyond what is named, the Katyn executions of 1940, the Hunger Plan, the Ukrainian War of Independence's battle-by-battle detail.
